The course was heavy for a 1st year student. Maybe not theoreticcaly, but definetely practically. The lab assignments required way more time than expected, usually up to 9-10 hours per week. The reason behind this is the fact that students were not taught about the lab assigntments. In almost all labs, we were given an objective that we had never accomplished nor taught before. We were expected to learn all the theory behind the lab by ourselves, and then put it into practice. This is definetely a lot for 1st year engineering students who does not have any background related to the labs. Moreover, we were also not taught about the coding language used in the course. Even though some examples were only slightly mentioned in lectures, we had to learn all the language by ourselves. It may be true that students had background in software engineering with previous CS courses, however when it comes to hardware languages we had no prior experience and it was edxtremely hard for most of us to learn the coding language, learn building circuits, learn the theory behind all of them all on our own and then combine them each week to come up with a lab assignment. I believe the course should either be removed to 2nd or 3rd year, or the students could be taught more about the lab assingments. For instance, instead of recitation hours, it would be highly beneficial to have lectures solely focused on VHDL programming and lab assignments. This way we could practice what we learned in the class more effectively. Finally, some labs were way before we learned the topic in the lectures. For example we were asked to build a circuit with 4-bit counters way before we were taught how counters work. The order of the labs could be revised to make them match with the topics learnt in class.

Let’s be clear: This wasn’t education. This was outsourcing. The university collected tuition for a course that functionally required students to design their own curriculum, source their own materials, and sacrifice their mental health—all while pretending this was somehow a valuable "independent learning" opportunity. Spoiler: It wasn’t. It was a waste of time, energy, and money. The fact that AI tools became a crutch for so many isn’t a reflection of student laziness; it’s damning evidence that the course provided no viable path to success.
The workload wasn’t just excessive—it was exploitative. Labs demanded hours of unpaid self-teaching, cannibalizing time needed for other courses, jobs, and basic human functioning. Meanwhile, the actual "instruction" was so disconnected from assessments that attending lectures felt like performance art. If the goal was to teach resilience in the face of institutional failure, congratulations: Mission accomplished.
In conclusion: This course was a masterclass in how not to educate. Future iterations should either commit to actual teaching or stop pretending to be anything more than a bureaucratic checkbox for degrees.

instructor:
The instructor presents the complicated mathematics of a topic before discussing its concepts and intuition, leaving many students too confused to even know what to ask. All the while, the instructor expects students to take good notes, which is unreasonable given that the instructor states half of the important info only verbally, and the he does not follow a pace that allows students to coherently take notes.
Without notes, students are left with the lecture slides, which are too hard to follow, with many half-explained equations and very few definitions or solved examples. And the supplementary textbooks are poor supplements because they often don’t approach topics like the instructor; they use different mathematical notation, or even NO maths. It takes too much time to connect this info with the slides. The same goes for online sources. So, with this lack of relevant learning material, many students manage to learn the course topics only by tripling their efforts while studying by themselves.
The learning being so inefficient makes the problem sets and quizzes much harder than they should be. And the problem sets are concerned not with teaching but only testing, providing no hints or any way to verify our solutions.
The term project has similar vagueness problems: it doesn’t even state the aim of doing projects, it doesn’t explain what we should have priority, and it expects us to make sophisticated informed decisions about machine learning techniques that we are yet to learn. It is inefficient to be forced to constantly ask assistants or to research ourselves when we don’t know what we don’t know.
Considering all this, instead of burdening students with so much preparation, beginner-friendly and directly relevant course material needs to be provided, such as handouts about the concepts of the ML techniques, and solved examples. This would help us prepare for lectures, be more informed when starting out on the term project, and get much less confused in general.

Finally: The project assumes that you know a lot about machine learning, but isn't this an introductory class? I mean, why are we expected to completely implement a neural network from scratch in this course where we only briefly kinda learn what a neural network is? I would be VERY confused if I didn't take an ML course before.
